item1.vignette: A 32-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding has fatigue and pica. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume is 70 fL, serum ferritin is low, and total iron-binding capacity is elevated.
item1.lead_in: Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
item1.tested_construct: Iron depletion limits heme synthesis, producing progressively microcytic hypochromic erythrocytes with low ferritin and increased iron-binding capacity.
item1.key_explanation: Chronic menstrual blood loss, pica, microcytosis, low ferritin, and elevated iron-binding capacity establish iron deficiency anemia.
item1.educational_objective: Diagnose iron deficiency anemia from characteristic clinical risk factors and iron studies.

item2.vignette: A 38-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding has fatigue, pica, microcytosis, low ferritin, and elevated TIBC.
item2.tested_construct: Depleted iron stores limit heme synthesis, producing microcytic hypochromic erythrocytes, low ferritin, and increased TIBC.
item2.key_explanation: Pica, microcytosis, low ferritin, and high TIBC strongly support iron deficiency.
item2.educational_objective: Differentiate iron deficiency from other microcytic anemias.

item1.system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
item1.vignette: A 35-year-old man develops tingling in his feet followed over 3 days by symmetric ascending leg weakness. Two weeks earlier he had a diarrheal illness. Deep-tendon reflexes are absent.
item1.lead_in: Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
item1.tested_construct: Acute immune-mediated peripheral nerve injury, often after infection, causes rapidly progressive symmetric weakness with hyporeflexia or areflexia and can impair respiratory muscles.
item1.key_explanation: Acute ascending symmetric weakness and areflexia after a gastrointestinal infection are classic for Guillain-Barré syndrome.
item1.educational_objective: Diagnose Guillain-Barré syndrome from postinfectious ascending weakness and areflexia.

item2.system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
item2.vignette: A 34-year-old man develops progressive ascending weakness and absent reflexes 10 days after a diarrheal illness.
item2.tested_construct: Acute immune-mediated peripheral nerve and root demyelination or axonal injury often follows infection and causes symmetric ascending weakness with areflexia.
item2.key_explanation: Postinfectious ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia is classic Guillain-Barré syndrome.

item1.vignette: A fatty meal enters the duodenum.
item1.lead_in: Which hormone most directly causes gallbladder contraction?
item1.tested_construct: Fat and amino acids in the duodenum stimulate I cells to release CCK, causing gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion.
item1.key_explanation: CCK released from duodenal and jejunal I cells in response to fat causes gallbladder contraction.
item1.educational_objective: Identify CCK as the mediator of gallbladder contraction after fat ingestion.

item2.vignette: A meal rich in fat and protein enters the duodenum. The gallbladder contracts, the sphincter of Oddi relaxes, and pancreatic acinar enzyme secretion increases.
item2.lead_in: Which gastrointestinal hormone is primarily responsible?
item2.tested_construct: Fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum/jejunum stimulate I cells to release CCK, which contracts the gallbladder, relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, and stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion.
item2.key_explanation: CCK is released from intestinal I cells in response to fats and amino acids. Its coordinated effects include gallbladder contraction, sphincter of Oddi relaxation, and increased pancreatic digestive-enzyme secretion.
item2.educational_objective: Identify CCK as the hormone coordinating bile delivery and pancreatic enzyme secretion after a fat- and protein-rich meal.

item1.vignette: A 15-year-old boy has recurrent syncope during sprinting and intense emotional stress. His resting ECG and echocardiogram are normal. Exercise testing provokes frequent ventricular ectopy followed by bidirectional ventricular tachycardia. Genetic testing identifies a gain-of-function pathogenic variant in RYR2.
item1.lead_in: Which of the following cellular events most directly triggers this patient's ventricular arrhythmias during adrenergic stimulation?

options.A: Diastolic sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium leak that activates sodium-calcium exchange and produces delayed afterdepolarizations
options.B: Prolonged ventricular action potentials that generate early afterdepolarizations during phase 3
options.C: Reduced fast sodium current that markedly slows ventricular phase 0 depolarization
options.D: Failure of ATP-sensitive potassium channels to open during myocardial ischemia
options.E: Spontaneous phase 4 depolarization caused by increased funny current in sinoatrial nodal cells

item1.tested_construct: Gain-of-function RYR2 variants destabilize the cardiac ryanodine receptor during adrenergic stimulation, causing inappropriate diastolic calcium leak from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; calcium overload activates the sodium-calcium exchanger and generates delayed afterdepolarizations that trigger bidirectional or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.
item1.key_explanation: RYR2 encodes the principal cardiac sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium-release channel. CPVT-associated gain-of-function variants make RyR2 abnormally leaky during catecholaminergic stimulation. Diastolic calcium overload activates the sodium-calcium exchanger, generating delayed afterdepolarizations and triggered ventricular activity.
item1.educational_objective: Explain RYR2-related CPVT as catecholamine-dependent diastolic sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium leak leading to sodium-calcium-exchanger-mediated delayed afterdepolarizations.

item2.vignette: A 15-year-old boy has recurrent syncope during intense exercise and emotional stress. Resting ECG and echocardiography are normal. Exercise testing produces frequent ventricular ectopy that progresses to bidirectional ventricular tachycardia. Genetic testing identifies a gain-of-function variant in RYR2.
item2.lead_in: Which cellular abnormality most directly promotes this patient's arrhythmia?

options.A: Persistent inward sodium current during ventricular repolarization
options.B: Reduced rapid delayed-rectifier potassium current during phase 3
options.C: Reduced funny current in sinoatrial nodal cells
options.D: Spontaneous diastolic calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
options.E: Failure of gap-junction formation between ventricular myocytes

item2.tested_construct: Gain-of-function RYR2 variants destabilize the cardiac ryanodine receptor and promote spontaneous diastolic calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum during adrenergic stimulation. The resulting inward current through the sodium-calcium exchanger can trigger delayed afterdepolarizations and polymorphic or bidirectional ventricular tachycardia.
item2.key_explanation: RYR2 encodes the cardiac sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium-release channel. Gain-of-function variants cause catecholamine-dependent spontaneous diastolic calcium release, promoting delayed afterdepolarizations and characteristic exercise- or emotion-triggered ventricular tachycardia.
item2.educational_objective: Connect RYR2-related CPVT to catecholamine-triggered diastolic sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium leak and delayed afterdepolarization-mediated ventricular arrhythmia.

item1.vignette: A 66-year-old man has fatigue, paresthesias, and impaired vibration sense. Laboratory studies show macrocytic anemia and hypersegmented neutrophils.
item1.lead_in: Which metabolite is most likely elevated because of this vitamin deficiency?
item1.tested_construct: Vitamin B12 deficiency impairs methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase reactions, producing defective DNA synthesis and accumulation of methylmalonic acid with neurologic injury.
item1.key_explanation: Vitamin B12 is required for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; deficiency therefore raises methylmalonic acid and can produce neurologic deficits.
item1.educational_objective: Distinguish vitamin B12 deficiency biochemically by elevated methylmalonic acid in a patient with macrocytic anemia and neurologic findings.

item2.vignette: A 68-year-old vegan has macrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, paresthesias, and impaired vibration sense.
item2.lead_in: Which metabolite is expected to be elevated?
item2.tested_construct: Vitamin B12 deficiency impairs methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, causing megaloblastic anemia plus neurologic injury from methylmalonic acid accumulation and myelin dysfunction.
item2.key_explanation: B12 deficiency impairs methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and elevates methylmalonic acid.
item2.educational_objective: Differentiate vitamin B12 from folate deficiency using methylmalonic acid and neurologic findings.

item1.system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
item1.vignette: A 31-year-old woman has ptosis and diplopia that worsen late in the day and improve after rest. Sensation and reflexes are normal.
item1.lead_in: The most common antibodies in this disorder target which structure?

options.C: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in smooth muscle
options.D: Voltage-gated sodium channels at nodes of Ranvier
options.E: Dopamine D2 receptors in the striatum

item1.tested_construct: Autoantibodies most often target postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, reducing functional receptor density and producing fatigable skeletal-muscle weakness.
item1.key_explanation: Most myasthenia gravis is caused by antibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
item1.educational_objective: Connect fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness with antibody-mediated loss of postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors.

item2.system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
item2.vignette: A 31-year-old woman has ptosis and diplopia that worsen late in the day and improve after rest. Reflexes and sensation are normal.
item2.lead_in: Which structure is primarily targeted in the most common form?
item2.tested_construct: Autoantibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors or related proteins reduce the safety factor for neuromuscular transmission and cause fatigable weakness.
item2.key_explanation: Most generalized myasthenia gravis is caused by antibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors.
item2.educational_objective: Identify the postsynaptic target in myasthenia gravis.

item1.vignette: A new screening test is evaluated in 100 people who are known by a reference standard to have a disease. The screening test is positive in 90 of them and negative in 10.
item1.lead_in: What is the sensitivity of the screening test?

options.D: Cannot be calculated without knowing disease prevalence

item1.tested_construct: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive: true positives divided by all people who truly have disease.
item1.key_explanation: Sensitivity = true positives / (true positives + false negatives) = 90/(90+10) = 90%.
item1.educational_objective: Calculate and interpret sensitivity from a 2×2 diagnostic-test table.

item2.vignette: A diagnostic test is evaluated in 200 people confirmed by a reference standard not to have the disease. The test is negative in 170 and positive in 30.
item2.lead_in: What is the specificity of the test?

options.E: Cannot be calculated without knowing the number of diseased patients

item2.tested_construct: Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative: true negatives divided by all people who truly do not have disease.
item2.key_explanation: Specificity = true negatives / (true negatives + false positives) = 170/(170+30) = 85%.
item2.educational_objective: Calculate specificity from disease-free subjects in a diagnostic-test validation study.

item1.vignette: A 2-year-old child has coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, corneal clouding, developmental delay, and skeletal deformities.
item1.lead_in: Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
item1.tested_construct: Alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency causes lysosomal accumulation of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate, producing coarse features, organomegaly, skeletal disease, and developmental decline.
item1.key_explanation: Hurler syndrome is caused by IDUA deficiency and glycosaminoglycan accumulation.
item1.educational_objective: Differentiate Hurler from Hunter syndrome using enzyme defect and corneal clouding.

item2.vignette: A boy has coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, joint stiffness, developmental delay, and no corneal clouding.
item2.lead_in: Which enzyme is deficient in this disorder?
item2.tested_construct: Iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency causes dermatan and heparan sulfate accumulation; unlike Hurler syndrome, corneal clouding is absent and inheritance is X-linked.
item2.key_explanation: Hunter syndrome is caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency and is inherited in an X-linked pattern.
item2.educational_objective: Identify iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency in Hunter syndrome.

item1.system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
item1.vignette: A 67-year-old man develops sudden vertigo, vomiting, hoarseness, and severe dysphagia. Examination shows left-sided facial loss of pain and temperature, right-sided body loss of pain and temperature, left limb ataxia, and left ptosis and miosis. Strength is preserved.
item1.lead_in: Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
item1.tested_construct: Lateral medullary ischemia, usually from vertebral or PICA territory disease, can injure the nucleus ambiguus, vestibular nuclei, inferior cerebellar peduncle, spinal trigeminal tract/nucleus, spinothalamic tract, and descending sympathetics, producing dysphagia/hoarseness, vertigo/ataxia, ipsilateral facial and contralateral body pain-temperature loss, and ipsilateral Horner syndrome.
item1.key_explanation: The combination of vertigo/ataxia, ipsilateral facial and contralateral body pain-temperature loss, ipsilateral Horner syndrome, and nucleus-ambiguus dysfunction causing dysphagia/hoarseness is classic lateral medullary syndrome.
item1.educational_objective: Recognize lateral medullary syndrome from crossed pain-temperature deficits, vestibulocerebellar findings, Horner syndrome, and nucleus ambiguus dysfunction.

item2.system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
item2.vignette: A 67-year-old man suddenly develops vertigo, vomiting, hoarseness, dysphagia, left facial loss of pain and temperature, right body loss of pain and temperature, left-sided ataxia, and left Horner syndrome. Limb strength is preserved.
item2.lead_in: Damage to which structure most directly explains the dysphagia and hoarseness?
item2.tested_construct: A lateral medullary infarct, usually involving vertebral or PICA territory, can damage the nucleus ambiguus, spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract, spinothalamic tract, descending sympathetic fibers, vestibular nuclei, and inferior cerebellar peduncle. Nucleus ambiguus injury causes dysphagia, hoarseness, and impaired gag/cough functions.
item2.key_explanation: The crossed sensory findings, ipsilateral Horner syndrome and ataxia, and preserved limb strength localize to the lateral medulla. Dysphagia and hoarseness specifically reflect involvement of the nucleus ambiguus and its CN IX/X branchial motor fibers.
item2.educational_objective: Localize dysphagia and hoarseness in lateral medullary syndrome to the nucleus ambiguus while integrating the syndrome's crossed sensory and sympathetic findings.

item1.vignette: A 16-year-old boy has progressive pain and swelling around the distal femur. Imaging shows a destructive metaphyseal lesion with a sunburst periosteal reaction.
item1.tested_construct: Malignant osteoblasts produce osteoid, commonly arising in metaphyses of long bones in adolescents.
item1.key_explanation: An adolescent with a metaphyseal destructive bone lesion and sunburst periosteal reaction has osteosarcoma.
item1.educational_objective: Recognize osteosarcoma from age, location, and radiographic pattern.

item2.vignette: A 14-year-old boy has fever and increasing thigh pain. Imaging shows a destructive diaphyseal femoral lesion with an onion-skin periosteal reaction.
item2.tested_construct: Ewing sarcoma is a malignant small round cell tumor of bone, often caused by EWSR1-FLI1 fusion, typically arising in the diaphysis of long bones or pelvis in children and adolescents.
item2.key_explanation: A painful diaphyseal bone tumor with onion-skin periosteal reaction in an adolescent is classic Ewing sarcoma.
item2.educational_objective: Differentiate Ewing sarcoma from osteosarcoma by age, location, and radiographic pattern.

item1.vignette: An adult has resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Plasma aldosterone is elevated and plasma renin activity is suppressed.
item1.lead_in: Which renal transport change most directly contributes to the hypokalemia in this disorder?

options.A: Reduced epithelial sodium-channel activity causing diminished lumen-negative potential
options.B: Increased epithelial sodium-channel-mediated sodium reabsorption in principal cells, enhancing potassium secretion into the lumen
options.C: Loss of NKCC2 activity causing loop-diuretic-like salt wasting
options.D: Loss of the distal Na+-Cl− cotransporter causing reduced distal sodium delivery
options.E: Reduced basolateral Na+-K+ ATPase activity in collecting-duct principal cells

item1.tested_construct: Autonomous aldosterone excess increases epithelial sodium-channel activity and basolateral Na+-K+ ATPase activity in collecting-duct principal cells, increasing sodium reabsorption and creating conditions that enhance renal potassium secretion; volume expansion suppresses renin and hydrogen-ion loss contributes to metabolic alkalosis.
item1.key_explanation: Aldosterone acts on principal cells to increase ENaC-mediated sodium entry and Na+-K+ ATPase activity. Increased sodium reabsorption makes the tubular lumen relatively negative and, together with increased intracellular potassium delivery from Na+-K+ ATPase, promotes potassium secretion through apical potassium channels. Autonomous aldosterone therefore causes hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and renin suppression.
item1.educational_objective: Connect primary aldosteronism with increased principal-cell ENaC activity and enhanced renal potassium secretion.

item2.vignette: A 43-year-old woman has resistant hypertension, muscle weakness, serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L, and metabolic alkalosis. Plasma renin activity is suppressed and aldosterone concentration is elevated.
item2.lead_in: Which renal change most directly contributes to this patient's hypokalemia?

options.A: Reduced proximal tubular sodium reabsorption causing bicarbonaturia
options.B: Reduced NKCC2 activity in the thick ascending limb
options.C: Reduced distal sodium delivery to collecting-duct principal cells
options.D: Increased ENaC-mediated sodium reabsorption in principal cells, increasing the electrical drive for potassium secretion
options.E: Inhibition of basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase in collecting-duct principal cells

item2.tested_construct: Autonomous aldosterone excess increases ENaC-mediated sodium entry in collecting-duct principal cells and enhances basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase activity, creating a lumen-negative potential that favors potassium secretion through ROMK. Aldosterone also promotes hydrogen secretion by alpha-intercalated cells, producing hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis while volume expansion suppresses renin.
item2.key_explanation: In primary hyperaldosteronism, aldosterone upregulates ENaC and Na+/K+-ATPase. Enhanced electrogenic sodium reabsorption makes the lumen more negative and drives potassium secretion, producing hypokalemia.
item2.educational_objective: Connect autonomous aldosterone excess to ENaC-mediated collecting-duct sodium reabsorption, potassium wasting, metabolic alkalosis, and suppressed renin.

item1.vignette: A healthy term newborn takes the first several breaths after delivery. Pulmonary blood flow rapidly increases, and a normal fetal interatrial shunt functionally closes.
item1.lead_in: Which of the following hemodynamic changes most directly causes this closure?

options.A: An increase in pulmonary vascular resistance that raises right-atrial pressure above left-atrial pressure
options.B: An increase in arterial oxygen tension that constricts the ductus arteriosus
options.C: Continued umbilical venous return that raises right-atrial preload after placental separation
options.D: A fall in pulmonary vascular resistance that increases pulmonary venous return and raises left-atrial pressure above right-atrial pressure
options.E: A fall in systemic vascular resistance caused by removal of the placental circulation

item1.tested_construct: With the first breaths, pulmonary vascular resistance falls and pulmonary blood flow increases. Increased pulmonary venous return raises left-atrial pressure above right-atrial pressure, pressing the septum primum against the septum secundum and functionally closing the foramen ovale.
item1.key_explanation: The first breaths expand the lungs and sharply reduce pulmonary vascular resistance. Pulmonary blood flow and pulmonary venous return to the left atrium therefore rise, while loss of placental venous return lowers right-sided filling. Once left-atrial pressure exceeds right-atrial pressure, the septum primum is pressed against the septum secundum, producing functional closure of the foramen ovale.
item1.educational_objective: Explain functional closure of the foramen ovale as a consequence of the postnatal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance and rise of left-atrial pressure above right-atrial pressure.

item2.vignette: A healthy term newborn takes the first several breaths after delivery. Within minutes, the flap valve of the foramen ovale is pushed closed against the interatrial septum.
item2.lead_in: Which hemodynamic change most directly produces this functional closure?

options.A: Right atrial pressure rises above left atrial pressure as pulmonary vascular resistance increases
options.B: Pulmonary vascular resistance rises and reduces pulmonary venous return
options.C: Systemic vascular resistance falls sharply after umbilical cord clamping
options.D: Right ventricular output bypasses the lungs through increased ductus arteriosus flow
options.E: Left atrial pressure rises above right atrial pressure as pulmonary venous return increases

item2.tested_construct: With the first breaths, pulmonary vascular resistance falls and pulmonary blood flow rises. Increased pulmonary venous return raises left atrial pressure. Simultaneously, loss of placental venous return reduces right-sided filling. The resulting left-to-right atrial pressure reversal presses the septum primum against the septum secundum, functionally closing the foramen ovale.
item2.key_explanation: The first breaths lower pulmonary vascular resistance, increase pulmonary blood flow, and raise pulmonary venous return to the left atrium. Left atrial pressure then exceeds right atrial pressure and pushes the septum primum closed.
item2.educational_objective: Explain functional closure of the foramen ovale as a consequence of postnatal pulmonary vasodilation and the resulting rise in left atrial pressure above right atrial pressure.

item1.vignette: In a randomized trial, the 5-year event rate is 20% with standard therapy and 10% with a new therapy.
item1.lead_in: What is the number needed to treat to prevent one additional event over 5 years?
item1.tested_construct: NNT is the reciprocal of absolute risk reduction and estimates how many patients need treatment to prevent one additional adverse outcome.
item1.educational_objective: Calculate number needed to treat from absolute event rates.

item2.vignette: In a randomized trial, the outcome occurs in 20% of participants receiving standard care and in 10% of participants receiving a new treatment over the same follow-up interval.
item2.lead_in: What is the number needed to treat to prevent one additional outcome?
item2.tested_construct: Number needed to treat is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction: NNT = 1 / (control event rate − treatment event rate), conventionally rounded up to the next whole patient when needed.
item2.key_explanation: The absolute risk reduction is 0.20 − 0.10 = 0.10. Number needed to treat is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction: 1 / 0.10 = 10. Thus, 10 patients must receive the new treatment over the stated interval to prevent one additional outcome compared with standard care.
item2.educational_objective: Calculate NNT as the reciprocal of absolute risk reduction.

item1.vignette: A newborn has polyhydramnios-associated prematurity, polyuria, poor weight gain, hypokalemia, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, elevated renin and aldosterone, and normal blood pressure. Newborn hearing testing shows bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Genetic testing identifies biallelic loss-of-function variants in BSND.
item1.lead_in: Which of the following transport abnormalities most directly explains the combination of renal salt wasting and hearing loss?

options.A: Loss of the apical Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb with normal inner-ear chloride-channel function
options.B: Impaired function and membrane localization of ClC-K chloride channels in renal and inner-ear epithelia due to loss of their barttin accessory subunit
options.C: Loss of the apical ROMK potassium channel in the thick ascending limb with preserved cochlear ion transport
options.D: Loss of the basolateral ClC-Kb channel alone in the distal nephron without impairment of ClC-Ka
options.E: Loss of the thiazide-sensitive NaCl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule

item1.tested_construct: Barttin, encoded by BSND, is an essential accessory beta subunit for ClC-Ka and ClC-Kb chloride channels in renal and inner-ear epithelia. Loss of barttin impairs basolateral chloride exit in the thick ascending limb and inner ear, causing severe renal salt wasting with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis and sensorineural deafness.
item1.key_explanation: BSND encodes barttin, an accessory subunit required for normal ClC-Ka/ClC-Kb chloride-channel function in the kidney and inner ear. Severe loss of barttin produces Bartter type IV: renal salt wasting with secondary hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism and hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, together with sensorineural deafness.
item1.educational_objective: Explain Bartter type IV as loss of barttin-dependent ClC-K chloride-channel function shared by kidney and inner ear.

item2.vignette: A 3-month-old boy is evaluated for poor weight gain, polyuria, and recurrent dehydration. He was born prematurely after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios. Laboratory studies show hypokalemia, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, and markedly elevated plasma renin and aldosterone concentrations; blood pressure is low-normal. Auditory brainstem testing confirms bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Genetic testing identifies biallelic pathogenic variants in BSND.
item2.lead_in: Which transport abnormality most directly explains the combination of this patient’s renal and auditory findings?

options.A: Impaired function of barttin-dependent ClC-Ka and ClC-Kb chloride channels in renal tubules and the inner ear
options.B: Impaired apical Na-K-2Cl cotransport caused by SLC12A1 dysfunction only in the thick ascending limb
options.C: Impaired apical ROMK potassium recycling caused by KCNJ1 dysfunction only in the thick ascending limb
options.D: Loss of the thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
options.E: Loss of epithelial sodium-channel activity in the collecting duct and secretory epithelia

item2.tested_construct: BSND encodes barttin, an essential beta subunit required for trafficking and function of ClC-Ka and ClC-Kb chloride channels. In the thick ascending limb, loss of barttin impairs basolateral chloride exit and salt reabsorption, producing renal salt wasting, secondary hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis and low-to-normal blood pressure. The same ClC-K channel complex in the inner ear explains congenital sensorineural hearing loss.
item2.key_explanation: Bartter syndrome type IV can result from BSND variants. Barttin is required for ClC-Ka/ClC-Kb chloride-channel function in renal tubules and potassium-secreting epithelia of the inner ear. Loss of this complex causes severe renal salt wasting with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis and sensorineural deafness.
item2.educational_objective: Link BSND/barttin dysfunction to impaired ClC-Ka/ClC-Kb channel function and recognize Bartter type IV from antenatal salt wasting plus sensorineural hearing loss.

item1.vignette: A child has polyuria, poor growth, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, high renin and aldosterone levels, and hypercalciuria. Genetic testing shows biallelic SLC12A1 variants.

options.A: Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
options.B: Epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct
options.C: Na-glucose cotransporter in the proximal tubule
options.D: Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb

item1.tested_construct: Loss of the thick ascending limb Na-K-2Cl cotransporter reduces sodium chloride reabsorption, producing salt wasting, secondary hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, and increased urinary calcium.
item1.key_explanation: SLC12A1 encodes NKCC2, the thick ascending limb sodium-potassium-2 chloride cotransporter; loss causes Bartter syndrome type 1.
item1.educational_objective: Relate Bartter syndrome type 1 to loss of NKCC2-mediated sodium chloride reabsorption in the thick ascending limb.

item2.vignette: A child has polyuria, poor growth, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, elevated plasma renin and aldosterone, and hypercalciuria with nephrocalcinosis. Genetic testing identifies biallelic pathogenic variants in SLC12A1.
item2.lead_in: Which nephron transport protein is directly affected in this disorder?

options.A: The apical Na+-Cl− cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
options.B: The epithelial sodium channel in collecting-duct principal cells
options.C: The apical Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
options.D: The basolateral Na+-K+ ATPase in proximal-tubule cells
options.E: The apical sodium-glucose cotransporter in the proximal tubule

item2.tested_construct: Loss of the apical Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransporter NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb impairs sodium chloride reabsorption, reduces the lumen-positive potential that normally drives paracellular calcium reabsorption, activates renin-aldosterone signaling, and produces hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with hypercalciuria.
item2.key_explanation: SLC12A1 encodes NKCC2, the apical Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransporter of the thick ascending limb. Loss of NKCC2 produces a loop-diuretic-like phenotype with renal salt wasting, renin/aldosterone activation, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, impaired concentrating ability, and increased urinary calcium because the lumen-positive voltage supporting paracellular calcium uptake is reduced.
item2.educational_objective: Identify NKCC2 loss in the thick ascending limb as the transport defect in type 1 Bartter syndrome.

item1.vignette: Hemophilic plasma lacking functional factor VIII or IX is exposed to concizumab. Free tissue factor pathway inhibitor falls, factor Xa generation during the initiation phase rises, and thrombin generation improves without replacement of the missing clotting factor.
item1.tested_construct: TFPI antagonism that enhances initiation-phase FXa generation
item1.key_explanation: Concizumab is a monoclonal antibody antagonist of endogenous TFPI. TFPI inhibition increases FXa generation during coagulation initiation and improves thrombin generation.
item1.educational_objective: Recognize hemostatic rebalancing by inhibition of an endogenous anticoagulant rather than replacement of a deficient procoagulant factor.

item2.vignette: Plasma from a patient with hemophilia is exposed to concizumab-mtci. Free tissue factor pathway inhibitor decreases, factor Xa generation during coagulation initiation rises, and thrombin generation improves without replacing factor VIII or IX.
item2.lead_in: Which direct action best explains these findings?

options.A: Antagonism of tissue factor pathway inhibitor

item2.tested_construct: TFPI antagonism enhancing factor Xa and thrombin generation
item2.key_explanation: Concizumab-mtci is a monoclonal antibody antagonist of endogenous tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI). TFPI inhibition enhances factor Xa production during coagulation initiation, improving thrombin generation and clot formation.
item2.educational_objective: Recognize TFPI antagonism as a rebalancing strategy that increases factor Xa and thrombin generation without replacing deficient clotting factors.

item1.vignette: Acidic chyme enters the duodenum after a meal.
item1.lead_in: Which hormone most directly increases pancreatic bicarbonate secretion?
item1.tested_construct: Acid entering the duodenum stimulates S cells to release secretin, which increases pancreatic and biliary bicarbonate secretion to neutralize gastric acid.
item1.key_explanation: Secretin is released by duodenal S cells in response to acid and stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion.
item1.educational_objective: Identify secretin as the major hormone driving pancreatic bicarbonate release.

item2.vignette: Acidic chyme enters the duodenum after a meal. Shortly afterward, pancreatic juice becomes markedly enriched in bicarbonate.
item2.lead_in: Which hormone most directly mediates this response?
item2.tested_construct: Acid entering the duodenum stimulates S cells to release secretin. Secretin activates Gs-coupled receptors on pancreatic ductal/centroacinar cells, increasing cAMP and secretion of bicarbonate-rich fluid.
item2.key_explanation: Duodenal acid releases secretin from S cells. Secretin signals through cAMP to pancreatic ductal/centroacinar cells, increasing bicarbonate and water secretion that neutralize gastric acid.
item2.educational_objective: Identify secretin as the principal hormonal stimulus for bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion after acid enters the duodenum.
